Sweeping tends to push fine dust around and grind it in, so skip the broom: go over the floor with a vacuum on the hard-floor setting (beater bar off) or a dry microfiber mop, flipping the pad as it loads. Then one pass with a well wrung-out, barely damp microfiber mop, dried right behind it, since standing water is what hurts hardwood. Sam's sweeping is a very normal way to make it worse, and I'm happy to keep talking about the kitchen stuff too.
Action: Stay here and listen; I won't order anything unless you say so.

A cardboard fort is a great pick. Beyond the basement boxes you'll want a box cutter or sturdy scissors (adult-only), packing or duct tape, markers for windows and doors, blankets and clips for a roof, and a flashlight for the inside. Doing the cutting tonight means tomorrow after school is all building.
Action: Save a fort checklist to your notes with the items to grab from the basement; nothing to order unless something turns out to be missing.

Start getting quotes about a month before the renewal date so you have time to compare, and don't cancel the old policy until the new one is confirmed in writing, so you're never uninsured. For cancelling, your insurer will want notice and may charge a fee if you cancel mid-term; at renewal it's usually simpler, but I'd confirm the exact terms in your policy rather than guess. Sending the school council reply first.

Try: 'If a payout fails because of a bank-side error, the system shall automatically reinitiate the payout without merchant intervention.' It keeps the 'shall', drops the nested clauses, and cuts the 'being required' wording. If you want a retry limit, that reads better as its own sentence.

Short version: screens in the hour before bed matter more than total screen time. In a 2025 study of 1,200 kids aged 6 to 9, those on a screen in the last 60 minutes fell asleep about 19 minutes later, worst with handhelds held close and least with a shared TV; the causes are light delaying melatonin, games and short video keeping kids wired, and screens pushing out wind-down routines. The fix is a fixed screens-off time an hour before bed (weekends too), devices charged in the kitchen and reading instead, which brought sleep back to normal within two weeks.
Action: Nothing to do unless you want me to add a screens-off time to Leo's routine.

A cohort retention curve is usually called flat when the period-over-period drop stays under about 1 to 2 percentage points for three or more periods in a row. Check several cohorts on the same axis from period 0 so one noisy cohort doesn't fool you, and see whether newer cohorts flatten higher or lower than older ones.
Action: If you send the curve or the Looker link, I'll check it against that rule.
